Even if they managed to get it all done, there was no way for Leon to get out of the end gate short of breaking those stupid cuffs off, or else wait for Herman to send him back through the Fog the old-fashioned way. And with how badly those static blasts were being focused and funneled through the furniture, there was no guarantee what shape he’d even be in at that point. So, it would have to be a tool hunt, then. Though with all the random toolboxes in this place that he had found over the trials, Jake had never once seen something actually USEFUL for something like this. No crowbars. No wire cutters. Not even a broken scalpel. The Entity didn’t leave them with what they needed. Just what she thought might be entertaining. “Of course she wouldn’t,” he muttered. “Not her style. Flashlights that barely work, medkits that run out before you stop bleeding, but the second you need something practical— ” Both men seemed to come to the same conclusion, shared across a look. They needed the keys. Jake looked at the door. Then at Leon. “I’ll find them.” Leon managed a faint smirk — but it faded quickly, buried under the tension winding back into his shoulders. He nodded, closed his eyes, and waited for the air to shift again, tracking Jake’s footfalls until they faded down the hallway. Chapter 3: Conductive Reasoning Jake had stopped checking his surroundings three drawers ago. Probably not the best call, all things considered. But after the fifth tray of shattered glass and bent syringes, the paranoia had dulled into background noise. Every cabinet, cart, and table in this wing had offered nothing but rusted scalpels, cracked syringes, and bandage rolls that looked like they’d been soaked in something before the Fog found them. It wasn’t even creepy anymore. Just tedious. Nothing had jumped him yet, and if Herman was still busy lighting up the far end of the map, that bought him time. Not comfort. Just time. He slammed another drawer shut, the metal shrieking in protest, and ripped open the next one. More gauze. Rusted scalpels tangled like brittle weeds. A blood pressure cuff half-melted to the lining. “ They’re just keys, ” he muttered, rifling with increasing irritation. “How hard is it to find a set of fucking keys? What are they, an inch wide? Half an inch? What, do they disintegrate if you make eye contact with them?” The next drawer had old notebooks — pages torn and curling with moisture, most of the ink blurred beyond recognition. He flipped one open on reflex. Mold across the spine. The few pages still intact were stained with dark splashes that could’ve been ink. Could’ve been blood. Hard to tell anymore. Everything the Fog touched decayed in stages. Wood splintered. Paper decayed. Even metal rusted faster than it had any right to. He tossed it aside and turned to the next tray when a scream knifed through the walls. He froze. One clean rip of pain, sharp enough to echo down through the vents. He crouched instinctively, angling himself toward the hallway’s edge and holding still. Leon. The lights above him buzzed faintly, a flicker of static skipping down the line like a warning. No footsteps followed. No voices. Just the distant groan of the building settling in its chains, and the faint crackle of static in the overhead lights. Jake exhaled slow through his nose, grounding himself with a palm against the floor. A single jolt like that wasn’t part of a chase. That meant Herman was still near Leon — and nowhere near here. He rubbed a hand down his face and stood. If Leon was still screaming, it meant he was still alive. If he was alive, Jake still had time. And he wasn’t wasting it. Jake spotted Meg two rooms over, crouched beside a battered generator that was audibly wheezing under the strain of whatever makeshift repairs she was forcing on it. Her sleeves were rolled up past her elbows, grease smudged along one cheek, fingers working fast inside the open panel. She didn’t even look up. He approached slowly, boots scuffing tile just loud enough to not startle — or so he thought. The second his hand touched her shoulder, she jolted like he’d set her on fire. “Shit—!” Meg yelped, slapping a live wire aside just before it could spark against the casing. “ What?! What could you POSSIBLY want that needs scaring a person so bad?!” Jake held up both hands, voice low. “We have a problem.” Meg glared, but stilled. “The Doctor has Leon locked down in one of the rooms near the main gen cluster,” he said quietly. “I need you to stay clear of that entire side of the building.” She blinked once, then rolled her eyes and dove back into the wires. “You’d have me leave that bastard a perfect patrol path when we’re this close to done?” she snapped, voice curt. “I don’t think so. We need at least one — maybe two — of those gens online or we’re never getting the gate. I’m headed that way as soon as I’m done here. You should be too. ” “No, Meg. You don’t get it. ” Jake took a step closer, lowering his voice. “Leon’s over there getting wrecked by static every time someone runs past. You need to stay the hell away.” “He knows what he signed up for,” Meg muttered, not looking at him. “He’ll live. Guy’s tough as nails. I think he’ll forgive a few shocks and a little panic if it gets the doors open faster.” Jake grit his teeth. “Meg, he’s cuffed to the furniture . He can’t leave the blast radius.” That stopped her.
